text: investors believed the internet was going
to change the world.
They were right.
But that didn't stop trillions of
dollars in market value from disappearing.
Companies collapsed.
Investors lost fortunes.
And one of the greatest technological
revolutions in history became associated with
one of its most spectacular financial disasters.
More than two decades later,
another technological revolution is attracting extraordinary
amounts of money.
Artificial intelligence.
Technology giants are constructing enormous data
centres.
Semiconductor companies are selling advanced processors.
Investors are betting on a future
where intelligent machines transform nearly every industry.
But beneath this historic investment boom
lies an uncomfortable question.
Is humanity building its next great
economic revolution,
or repeating one of its most
expensive financial mistakes?
To understand the answer,
we need to travel back to
a time when the internet was
still new.
During the early 1990s,
the internet began transforming from a
relatively specialized network into something ordinary
people could access.
For the first time,
businesses could communicate with customers around
the world without opening physical stores
in every country.
Information could travel almost instantly.
Entire industries suddenly appeared vulnerable to disruption.
Entrepreneurs recognized an enormous opportunity.
Online shopping,
digital advertising,
internet banking and electronic communication promised
to change the way economies operated.
Investors wanted to be part of
that future.
Money began flowing into internet companies
at an extraordinary pace.
But something unusual happened.
Instead of valuing businesses primarily on
their profits,
investors increasingly valued them on their potential.
Website visitors,
user growth and market share became
important indicators of success,
even when companies were losing money.
Many businesses believed that profitability could
come later.
The immediate priority was expansion.
Imagine launching an online store that
loses money on every order.
Under normal circumstances,
investors would question whether such a
business could survive.
But during the dot-com boom,
rapid expansion could attract additional investment
and push a company's valuation even higher.
The expectation was that once the
company became large enough,
profits would eventually follow.
Sometimes,
that expectation was reasonable.
Sometimes,
it was little more than speculation.
And as stock prices continued rising,
distinguishing between the two became increasingly difficult.
By the beginning of 2000,
enthusiasm surrounding internet companies had reached
extraordinary levels.
The Nasdaq Composite,
heavily influenced by technology stocks,
had climbed approximately 86% during 1999 alone.
But beneath the rising stock prices,
many businesses were struggling.
They were spending enormous amounts of
money on advertising,
employees and infrastructure without generating enough
revenue to sustain themselves.
Their survival depended on investors continuing
to provide capital.
Then confidence began to disappear.
Investors became increasingly concerned about company
valuations and profitability.
Stock prices started falling.
For businesses that depended on external
financing,
declining investor confidence became an existential threat.
Without fresh capital,
they could no longer finance their operations.
Companies began shutting down.
Employees lost their jobs.
Investors watched their savings evaporate.
Between its peak in March 2000
and the subsequent market bottom in
the Nasdaq lost roughly 77% of
its value.
Imagine investing $10,000 near the peak
in a portfolio that tracked the index.
Ignoring dividends and fees,
that investment would have fallen to
approximately $2,300.
Yet something remarkable happened after the crash.
The internet continued growing.
Online shopping expanded.
Digital advertising became increasingly important.
Businesses built successful models around technologies
that had once attracted excessive speculation.
The internet was not the illusion.
The unrealistic financial expectations surrounding many
internet companies were.
And that distinction is essential to
understanding artificial intelligence today.
The modern AI boom accelerated dramatically
following the introduction of widely accessible
generative AI systems.
Suddenly,
ordinary people could interact with machines
capable of generating text,
writing software,
creating images and assisting with complex tasks.
Businesses began exploring how artificial intelligence
could improve productivity,
reduce costs and create entirely new services.
Technology companies recognized a potentially enormous market.
But artificial intelligence requires more than software.
Behind every advanced AI system lies
a vast physical infrastructure.
Specialized processors perform enormous numbers of calculations.
Servers operate inside sophisticated data centres.
Cooling systems prevent equipment from overheating.
Electricity networks supply the energy necessary
to keep these facilities running.
Building this infrastructure requires substantial investment.
In November 2026,
the European Central Bank highlighted estimates
suggesting that cumulative capital expenditure by
seven major American technology companies could
reach approximately $5.5 trillion by 2030.
That is a forecast,
not money that has already been
spent,
and it includes broader company investment
rather than exclusively AI expenditure.
Nevertheless,
it illustrates the extraordinary scale of
the expansion.
Companies are spending today because they
expect AI services to generate substantial
economic value tomorrow.
But spending money and earning profitable
returns on that money are two
very different things.
To understand the financial risks,
imagine a simplified artificial intelligence economy.
A semiconductor manufacturer produces advanced computing chips.
A cloud computing company purchases those
chips and installs them inside a
data centre.
An AI developer rents computing capacity
from that cloud company to train
and operate its models.
Finally,
businesses and individual customers pay to
use the resulting AI services.
Money moves through the system,
supporting revenue at every stage.
When customer demand expands,
the entire network can benefit.
Chip manufacturers sell more processors.
Cloud companies rent more computing capacity.
AI developers attract more customers.
And investors anticipate higher future profits.
But what happens when businesses within
this ecosystem also finance one another?
Imagine a chip manufacturer investing $1 billion
in an AI developer.
That developer uses part of its
funding to purchase computing services.
The computing provider then purchases more
chips from the original manufacturer.
Each company may benefit from the
resulting activity.
But analysts must ask how much
demand is ultimately supported by paying
customers,
rather than continued financing from within
the industry itself.
Such arrangements do not automatically indicate
fraud or financial manipulation.
Strategic partnerships can help businesses develop
useful technologies.
However,
they make it especially important to
examine the underlying sources of revenue.
Because ultimately,
the entire investment chain must generate
enough external economic value to support
the money being invested.
Otherwise,
the system becomes increasingly dependent on
expectations about the future.
And expectations can change frighteningly quickly.
Another important development is the way
AI infrastructure is being financed.
Imagine a technology company that generates
$10 billion in operating cash flow.
After spending $6 billion on buildings,
equipment and other capital investments,
it has approximately $4 billion remaining
under a simplified definition of free
cash flow.
Now imagine its investment requirements rise
to $14 billion while operating cash
flow remains unchanged.
Its free cash flow becomes negative.
The company must use existing cash
reserves,
sell assets,
raise equity or borrow money to
cover the difference.
In October 2026,
the International Monetary Fund highlighted the
increasing use of debt across the
AI ecosystem and warned that disappointing
returns could place additional pressure on
financing arrangements.
This matters because debt creates obligations
that do not disappear simply because
customer demand weakens.
Lenders still expect repayment.
Interest payments must still be made.
And long-term financial commitments can remain
in place even when technology becomes outdated.
Consider a data centre financed with
a long-term loan.
If newer processors make its equipment
less competitive before the investment has
earned back its original cost,
the owner could face financial difficulties.
The technology may have improved.
But the economics of the original
investment may have deteriorated.
This creates a fundamental tension between
the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence
and the financial commitments required to
build its infrastructure.
The answer depends on how we
measure the size of a bubble.
Are we measuring the amount of
infrastructure being built?
The market value of technology companies?
The amount of debt supporting the expansion?
Or the difference between company valuations
and their underlying economic value?
These measurements can produce very different answers.
Research cited by the European Central
Bank in November 2026 estimated that
annual AI investment requirements could exceed
3% of American economic output over
the investment period.
For comparison,
investment during the internet boom was
estimated at approximately 1.1%.
These are not perfectly equivalent historical
measurements,
and the AI figures depend on forecasts.
Nevertheless,
they suggest that today's infrastructure expansion
could be considerably larger relative to
the economy.
But larger investment does not automatically
mean a larger financial bubble.
A railway connecting productive cities may
require enormous investment and still generate
substantial long-term returns.
An expensive railway connecting places with
insufficient demand may become a financial disaster.
The critical question is not simply
how much money is being spent.
It is whether the economic returns
will justify that spending.
There are several important differences between
the dot-com era and the current
AI boom.
Many of the internet startups that
attracted extraordinary valuations during the late
1990s had weak business models and
limited financial resources.
Today,
several of the largest companies investing
in artificial intelligence already operate highly
profitable businesses.
They generate revenue from cloud computing,
advertising,
software,
subscriptions and digital commerce.
This gives them resources that many
speculative dot-com companies never possessed.
Artificial intelligence also has practical applications
that extend beyond future promises.
Businesses are already using AI systems
to assist with software development,
customer support,
research and administrative work.
These applications can create genuine economic benefits.
However,
profitable companies can still make unprofitable investments.
And a useful technology does not
guarantee attractive returns for every company
involved in developing it.
During the internet boom,
businesses constructed extensive fibre-optic networks to
prepare for future internet traffic.
Some infrastructure investments were financially unsuccessful
because demand developed more slowly than expected.
Yet those networks eventually helped support
the expansion of the digital economy.
It is entirely possible that artificial
intelligence follows a similar pattern.
Society could benefit enormously from infrastructure
that produces disappointing financial returns for
some of its original investors.
Technological success and investment success are
not necessarily the same thing.
Imagine that AI adoption continues growing,
but customers are unwilling to pay
enough to justify the industry's enormous investments.
Cloud companies may reduce their expansion plans.
Semiconductor manufacturers may receive fewer orders.
Data centre developers may struggle to
attract tenants.
Businesses with substantial financial obligations could
face increasing pressure.
Investors would begin revising their expectations.
And because financial markets anticipate future
earnings,
company valuations could fall before the
full economic consequences become visible.
The effects might extend beyond technology companies.
Retirement funds,
investment portfolios and financial institutions hold
exposure to technology-related assets.
Construction companies,
electricity providers and equipment manufacturers may
also depend on continued infrastructure expansion.
But a collapse is not inevitable.
Demand could grow sufficiently to justify
the investments.
Technological improvements could reduce operating costs.
New applications could create revenue streams
that are difficult to anticipate today.
The investment boom could also experience
a gradual adjustment rather than a
dramatic crash.
The future depends on how these
competing forces develop.
The dot-com bubble demonstrated that investors
can correctly identify a revolutionary technology
and still misunderstand its financial value.
The internet changed the world.
But not every internet company deserved
its valuation.
Artificial intelligence may also transform the
global economy.
It could reshape industries,
create new businesses and fundamentally alter
how people work.
Yet none of that eliminates the
possibility of excessive speculation,
overinvestment or disappointing returns.
The most important question is not
whether artificial intelligence is useful.
It is whether the profits generated
by artificial intelligence will ultimately justify
the extraordinary financial commitments being made today.
History does not tell us exactly
what will happen next.
But it reminds us that even
the most convincing vision of the
future can become dangerous when financial
expectations move too far ahead of
economic reality.
The dot-com generation learned that lesson
the hard way.
Whether the artificial intelligence generation will
learn it differently remains one of
the most important financial questions of
our time.
This is The Epoch Ledger.
Understanding the past.
Decoding the present.
